nodes.title: Invariant subspaces

nodes.title: Equivalence

nodes.title: Complete reducibility

nodes.title: Maschke theorem

nodes.title: Schur lemma
nodes.description: Schur's lemma constrains intertwiners between irreducible representations. Over an algebraically closed field in finite dimensions, irreducible endomorphisms are scalar.

nodes.title: Semisimple modules

nodes.title: Characters of finite groups

nodes.title: Character theory
nodes.description: Characters encode representations by traces of their operators. Over the complex numbers for finite groups, they determine decompositions efficiently.

nodes.title: Traces
nodes.description: The trace of the representing matrix defines the character at a group element. It is invariant under change of basis and conjugation.

nodes.title: Orthogonality relations
nodes.description: Irreducible complex characters are orthonormal for the normalized class-function inner product. These relations give multiplicity formulas.

nodes.title: Regular character
nodes.description: The regular representation acts on functions or the group algebra by translation. Its character reveals that each irreducible occurs with multiplicity equal to its dimension.

nodes.title: Character computations
nodes.description: Character tables collect the irreducible trace data of a finite group. Conjugacy and orthogonality constrain their entries.

nodes.title: Conjugacy classes
nodes.description: Characters are constant on conjugacy classes. These classes therefore index the columns of a character table.

nodes.title: Character tables

nodes.title: Decomposition of representations

nodes.title: Induction, restriction, and products

nodes.title: Induced representations
nodes.description: Induction builds a group representation from a representation of a subgroup. Reciprocity relates this construction to restriction.

nodes.title: Cosets and induced modules
nodes.description: Induced modules combine coset data with the original subgroup action. Tensoring over the subgroup algebra gives an intrinsic construction.

nodes.title: Frobenius reciprocity
nodes.description: Frobenius reciprocity identifies suitable intertwiner spaces for induction and restriction. It turns one multiplicity problem into another.

nodes.title: Examples

nodes.title: Operations on representations

nodes.title: Tensor products

nodes.title: Symmetric powers

nodes.title: Restriction and decomposition

nodes.title: Representations of compact groups

nodes.title: Invariant integration
nodes.description: Compactness permits invariant averaging through Haar measure. This replaces finite summation and produces invariant geometric structures.

nodes.title: Haar measure motivation
nodes.description: Haar measure supplies translation-invariant integration on a compact group. Normalization gives total mass one and makes averaging possible.

nodes.title: Averaging inner products
nodes.description: Averaging an inner product over a compact group produces an invariant positive inner product. Finite-dimensional continuous representations therefore become unitary.

nodes.title: Complete reducibility
nodes.description: Orthogonal complements of invariant subspaces are invariant for unitary representations. This proves finite-dimensional complete reducibility for compact groups.

nodes.title: Peter–Weyl theory
nodes.description: Peter–Weyl theory decomposes functions on compact groups using matrix coefficients. It generalizes Fourier series beyond abelian groups.

nodes.title: Matrix coefficients
nodes.description: A matrix coefficient evaluates a representation between chosen vectors. These scalar functions retain the group's linear action data.

nodes.title: Fourier decomposition

nodes.title: Compact-group examples

nodes.title: Lie groups and Lie algebras
nodes.description: Lie groups combine a smooth manifold with compatible group operations. The Lie bracket records infinitesimal noncommutativity.

nodes.title: Smooth groups
nodes.description: Lie groups combine a smooth manifold with compatible group operations. Differentiation converts their local symmetry into linear data.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Matrix groups
nodes.description: Matrix Lie groups are smooth groups realized inside invertible matrices. They provide explicit examples and formulas for the general theory.

nodes.title: Tangent space at identity
nodes.description: The tangent space at the identity carries the Lie algebra structure. Translation identifies tangent information at other group points with this space.

nodes.title: Exponential map
nodes.description: The exponential map follows one-parameter subgroups from tangent vectors. It relates the Lie algebra to a neighborhood of the group identity.

nodes.title: Lie algebra structure
nodes.description: The Lie bracket records infinitesimal noncommutativity. Adjoint actions and one-parameter subgroups connect this structure back to the group.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Brackets
nodes.description: A Lie bracket is bilinear, antisymmetric, and satisfies the Jacobi identity. For matrix Lie algebras it is the commutator.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Adjoint representation
nodes.description: The adjoint representation differentiates conjugation to an action on the Lie algebra. It links internal group symmetry to algebra automorphisms.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Integration of one-parameter subgroups
nodes.description: Each Lie algebra element generates a one-parameter subgroup of a Lie group. This integrates a constant infinitesimal direction into global motion.

nodes.title: Structure theory of Lie algebras
nodes.description: Solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras impose different restrictions on repeated brackets. Semisimple Lie algebras have no nonzero solvable ideals.

nodes.title: Solvable and nilpotent algebras
nodes.description: Solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras impose different restrictions on repeated brackets. Their representations admit strong triangularity results under appropriate field hypotheses.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Derived series
nodes.description: The derived series repeatedly takes brackets within the current algebra. Termination defines solvability.

nodes.title: Engel and Lie theorems
nodes.description: Engel's theorem concerns nilpotent operator actions, while Lie's theorem triangularizes representations of solvable algebras over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field. Their assumptions and conclusions should be kept distinct.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: Upper triangular and strictly upper triangular matrices illustrate solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras. Their bracket series make the distinction explicit.

nodes.title: Semisimple algebras
nodes.description: Semisimple Lie algebras have no nonzero solvable ideals. In characteristic zero, invariant bilinear forms expose their structure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Killing form
nodes.description: The Killing form is the trace pairing of adjoint operators. Its degeneracy reflects structural properties of the Lie algebra.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cartan criteria
nodes.description: Cartan criteria characterize semisimplicity and solvability through trace conditions in characteristic zero. They turn bracket structure into linear-algebra tests.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Decomposition principles
nodes.description: A semisimple Lie algebra decomposes into simple ideals over the standard characteristic-zero setting. This reduces classification to simple components.

nodes.title: The sl2 model and highest weights
nodes.description: The Lie algebra sl2 provides the basic model for highest-weight arguments. Highest-weight modules extend the sl2 pattern to semisimple Lie algebras.

nodes.title: sl2 representations
nodes.description: The Lie algebra sl2 provides the basic model for highest-weight arguments. Its finite-dimensional complex representations are controlled by elementary weight strings.

nodes.title: Raising and lowering operators
nodes.description: Raising and lowering operators move eigenvectors between neighboring weights. Their commutator relations constrain the allowed string lengths.

nodes.title: Weight strings
nodes.description: A weight string is a sequence of vectors linked by these operators. Finite-dimensionality forces the string to terminate at both ends.

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.description: Finite-dimensional irreducible sl2 representations are indexed by nonnegative integer highest weights. Each such weight determines a representation with one more dimension than the weight.

nodes.title: Highest-weight modules
nodes.description: Highest-weight modules extend the sl2 pattern to semisimple Lie algebras. Enveloping algebras and induced modules provide their algebraic construction.

nodes.title: Universal enveloping algebra
nodes.description: The universal enveloping algebra converts Lie algebra representations into associative-algebra modules. Its defining relations preserve the original bracket.

nodes.title: Verma modules
nodes.description: A Verma module is induced from a chosen highest-weight action of a Borel subalgebra. It is a universal starting point for highest-weight modules.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Finite-dimensional quotients
nodes.description: Dominant integral highest weights produce finite-dimensional irreducible quotients in the complex semisimple setting. Other weights generally do not yield finite-dimensional modules.

nodes.title: Root systems and Weyl groups

nodes.title: Cartan subalgebras
nodes.description: Cartan subalgebras provide simultaneous weight coordinates for semisimple structure. Roots describe the adjoint action in those coordinates.

nodes.title: Roots and weights

nodes.title: Root spaces
nodes.description: Root spaces are eigenspaces for the Cartan action. Their brackets and dimensions constrain the algebra's structure.

nodes.title: Reflections

nodes.title: Classification

nodes.title: Dynkin diagrams

nodes.title: Weyl groups

nodes.title: Simple Lie algebras

nodes.title: Dominant weights
nodes.description: Dominant integral weights label finite-dimensional irreducible representations of complex semisimple Lie algebras. Their lattice structure also controls tensor-product questions.

nodes.title: Weight lattices

nodes.title: Irreducible modules
nodes.description: Every finite-dimensional irreducible module has a highest weight in the dominant integral lattice. Conversely, each such weight determines one up to isomorphism.

nodes.title: Tensor products

nodes.title: Character formulae

nodes.title: Weyl character formula

nodes.title: Dimensions
nodes.description: The Weyl dimension formula follows by evaluating the character appropriately at the identity. It computes dimensions from positive roots and the highest weight.

nodes.title: Branching previews

nodes.title: Lie groups and global representation theory

nodes.title: From algebra to group
nodes.description: A Lie algebra representation describes only infinitesimal symmetry. Passing to a chosen Lie group also requires attention to its global topology.

nodes.title: Simply connected groups
nodes.description: Simply connected Lie groups eliminate the fundamental-group obstruction to integrating Lie algebra representations. They serve as universal group-level models for this step.

nodes.title: Integration
nodes.description: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra representation integrates uniquely to the connected simply connected group with that Lie algebra. The integrated representation recovers the original one by differentiation.

nodes.title: Global constraints

nodes.title: Compact and noncompact examples

nodes.title: Classical groups
nodes.description: General linear, orthogonal, symplectic, and related groups form the classical families. Their defining forms or determinant conditions reveal their basic symmetries.

nodes.title: Unitary representations
nodes.description: A unitary representation preserves an inner product, possibly on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. This condition makes analytic methods available.

nodes.title: Selected decomposition results

nodes.title: Further directions and applications

nodes.title: Flag varieties

nodes.title: Geometric ideas
